## 1. Intro

- Design Facebook Live comments; applies to any live-streaming platform
- "The second most popular question asked in Meta system design interviews"
  - Popular across all the big tech companies

## 2. Roadmap

- Six steps
  1. **Requirements**: functional (core features) and non-functional (qualities)
  2. **Core entities**: the nouns; often map to tables
     - No full schema yet: too early to know it
  3. **API**: core user-facing endpoints, exchanging the entities
  4. **Data flow**: for infra-heavy questions only; skipped here
  5. **High-level design**: boxes and arrows; only the functional requirements
  6. **Deep dives**: one by one through the non-functional requirements
     - Where senior and especially staff candidates show their worth

## 3. What FB Live Comments is

- Facebook Live: users stream video to their audience
- We design the comments under the stream
  - Viewers post comments while watching
  - Comments stream to all other viewers in near real time
- Same feature on TikTok Live, Instagram Live, Twitch, YouTube Live

## 4. Functional requirements

1. **Viewers can post a comment**
2. **Viewers see all comments in near real time**
   - New comments append to the list without a page refresh
3. **Viewers see comments posted before they joined**
   - Scroll up to load older ones
- Below the line: replying to comments; reacting to comments or the video
- Tip on "below the line"
  - Use it only when something comes up while brainstorming and you agree it's out
  - E.g., "should users reply?"; interviewer says no; now it's a contract

## 5. Non-functional requirements

- Statements like "the system should be able to…" / "the system should be…"
- Consider CAP, scalability, latency, durability, security, fault tolerance, compliance
  - Don't just list them; most systems need all of them
  - Call out what's uniquely relevant and what you'll prioritize
- 1. **Scale: millions of concurrent videos; thousands of comments/s per video**
  - Interviewer may give it or ask you to estimate
  - Fun fact: most popular FB Live video, "Chewbacca Mom," viewed 180M+ times
- 2. **Availability over consistency for comment creation (and reads)**
  - Strong consistency = every read sees the latest write
  - Not seeing the very latest comment isn't an error
  - Better to show comments than none
- 3. **Low-latency broadcast: ~200 ms**
  - Messi scores; comments five minutes later make no sense
  - ~200 ms is what humans perceive as real time; lower doesn't matter
  - Write-up: < 200 ms end-to-end under typical network conditions (write-up)
- Quantify where possible and put each in context
  - "Availability > consistency" alone is uninteresting; "for comment creation" says why
- Below the line: security (write-up: only authorized users post), integrity (spam, hate speech)

## 6. Core entities

- Should move quickly; not difficult here
- **Comment**
- **Live Video**: owned by another team, but we relate to it
- **User / viewer** (write-up: a user can be a viewer or a broadcaster)

## 7. API

- Formula: go through functional requirements one by one; an endpoint for each
  - Works for user-facing products; less so for something like a web crawler

```
POST /comments/:liveVideoId  -> 200
  body: Comment

GET  /comments/:liveVideoId?cursor={last_comment_id}&direction={after|before}&pageSize=50
```

- Post
  - POST: creating a resource
  - Pluralized resource name (proper REST; "who cares," but done)
  - liveVideoId in the path: required, so path parameter (body would also work)
  - Body is just the Comment entity; no need to detail fields yet
  - Write-up: userId comes from the JWT/session header, not the body, so users can't impersonate others (write-up)
- Real-time reads
  - Astute viewers know this needs a persistent connection; if you know, write it down
  - Evan starts simple: a GET with **cursor pagination**
    - Cursor = ID of a row; get the next page after it
    - Call repeatedly to simulate real time
  - OK even for staff to start this way; say it will become a persistent connection
- Older comments: same endpoint with `direction=before`
- Write-up shape: `GET /comments/:liveVideoId?cursor=…&pageSize=10&sort=desc` (write-up)

## 8. High-level design

- Go API by API: what happens in the backend, which components are needed
- Moves fast; the time belongs to deep dives

### 8.1 Post a comment

- Client, **API gateway** (not strictly needed; used for its middleware), **comment service**, **comments DB**
- Flow: POST, gateway forwards, service writes to DB, returns 200
- Now define the data model
  - Comment: commentId (PK), videoId, authorId, content, createdAt
  - Index on videoId (queried a lot); sort by createdAt
- DB choice deferred to scaling; any DB works for the HLD (SQL, key-value, document)
- Write-up picks DynamoDB: simple records, no complex relations or transactions (write-up)

### 8.2 New comments in near real time (polling first)

- Say upfront you know this needs a persistent connection, then start simple
- Client polls every 2–5 s: "comments since comment X?"
  - Time could also be the cursor; maybe more natural here
- SQL: `SELECT * FROM comments WHERE videoId = ? AND createdAt > <cursor createdAt>`
  - Similar on a document or key-value store
- Write-up: polling fast enough for "near real time" would mean every few ms; not feasible (write-up)

### 8.3 Comments before joining

- Same endpoint, `direction=before`; the comparison flips
- On join: load the video with the last ~50 comments
- Aside: optimizing scroll-up (not the focus; mention briefly)
  - Per-user cache keyed by user + videoId, holding ~1,000 recent comments with a tight TTL
    - Serve the next 50 from cache instead of querying
  - Or send 500; when the user nears the 400th, prefetch the next 500 (like Tinder)
  - Matters only for very busy videos
- Write-up: offset pagination is bad (write-up)
  - Counts through preceding rows; unstable when comments are added/removed (duplicates, gaps)
- Write-up: cursor pagination is great; DynamoDB query example (write-up)

```json
{ "TableName": "comments",
  "KeyConditionExpression": "liveVideoId = :liveVideoId AND commentId < :cursor",
  "ScanIndexForward": false, "Limit": "pageSize" }
```

- The HLD is a basic CRUD service, but it meets every functional requirement

## 9. Deep dive: low-latency broadcast (WebSocket vs SSE)

- Proactivity depends on level
  - Junior/mid: interviewer asks ("polling misses latency; what else?")
  - Senior/staff: you find the issues and drive
- Polling gives 2–5 s latency vs 200 ms target
- Key insight: push over a persistent connection instead of request/response
- **WebSockets**
  - Bidirectional: either side sends any time
  - Works: push new comments to clients
  - Own protocol: HTTP handshake, then upgrade
    - Every hop (gateway, LBs, proxies, firewalls) must support the upgrade
    - Often works in test, breaks in prod or for some users (corporate firewalls)
    - AWS API Gateway supports it; NGINX can be configured; doable, but overhead
  - Best when reads ≈ writes, like a messenger (see the WhatsApp video)
  - Live comments: mostly passive viewers; maybe ~1:1,000 writers to readers
  - So WebSockets are overkill
- **SSE (server-sent events)**: the pick
  - Persistent, **unidirectional**: server pushes, client can't send on it
  - Plain HTTP/HTTPS; headers say "chunks are coming"; looks like a long-running request
  - Browsers handle reconnection natively
  - Posting stays a normal HTTP POST
  - Caveat: some gateways close long connections after a set time; raise timeouts or set headers
  - Write-up adds: proxies/LBs may buffer streams; browsers limit SSE connections per domain; long connections are harder to monitor (write-up)
- How does the service know whom to push to?
  - **In-memory map** in the service, no DB state
  - On connect, the client says which video (e.g., in a header)

```
videoId1: [conn1, conn4, conn7]
videoId2: [conn2, conn3, conn5]
```

  - New comment for video 1: loop over its connections, `conn.send(comment)`
- Problem: horizontal scaling
  - The comment lands on server A; video 1's viewers are on server B

## 10. Deep dive: scale (realtime servers, dispatcher vs pub/sub)

- Do math when a decision needs it, not upfront for its own sake
  - Most candidates estimate, say "it's big," then design the same thing
- Bottleneck: SSE connections
  - 1M concurrent videos × ~1,000 viewers = ~1B connections
  - A high-powered box handles roughly 1M SSE connections ("give or take")
  - So ~**1,000 servers** just for connections
  - Write-up says commonly ~100K per server; CPU, memory, file descriptors limit first (write-up)
  - Write-up: 65,535 is the port range, not a connection limit (write-up)
- Split out a **realtime comment service**
  - Comment service keeps POST and history GETs (maybe ~100 instances)
  - Realtime service holds SSE connections (~1,000 instances)
  - Scale each independently
- Problem: the comment service must tell the right realtime servers about a new comment

### 10.1 Option A: central dispatcher with ZooKeeper

- ZooKeeper keeps a registry: servers, health, which videos each serves (with counts)
- On connect: ask "viewer of video 1, which server?"; get a host; open SSE there
- On new comment: look up which servers have video 1; call them; they push via their map
- Don't ask ZooKeeper every time
  - Comment service caches the mapping in memory
  - Subscribes to ZooKeeper updates to keep the cache fresh
- Downsides
  - Extra component, extra hop on connect (cache mostly hides it; "hand-waving")
  - Tracking server churn: registration, heartbeats, scale up/down, failures
  - Server state and ZooKeeper's view can drift: a consistency problem (tooling helps)

### 10.2 Option B: pub/sub broadcast

- The comment service "yells into the ether with a megaphone"
- Commit the comment to the DB first (durability), then publish to **pub/sub**
- All realtime servers subscribe
  - Each checks its map; if it has viewers of that video, it pushes; else ignores
- Upsides
  - No consistency issue: only realtime servers know their own state
  - Graceful failure: a server dies, viewers reconnect elsewhere, map rebuilds, still subscribed
- Verdict: both valid; Evan finds pub/sub simpler
  - FB Live in production used a dispatcher-style approach ("to my knowledge," not ZooKeeper), for scaling and co-location reasons
- Level read
  - Mid-level: "pub/sub from comment service to realtime service over SSE or WebSocket" is golden
  - Senior: weigh the trade-offs
  - Staff: pros and cons in detail, plus how each scales
- Write-up names the naive version "every server processes every comment" (Good) (write-up)

## 11. Deep dive: partitioned pub/sub and co-location

- Staff / great-senior topic
- Problem: every realtime server receives every comment ("drinking through a fire hose")
  - CPU wasted checking comments for videos it doesn't serve
- **Partition** the pub/sub into channels/topics
  - Channel = `hash(videoId) % N`
  - Servers subscribe only to channels for videos they serve
  - Not perfect: you also get other videos in the same hash group
- Don't do one channel per video
  - Wouldn't work in Kafka; Redis probably has limits too ("off the top of my head")
  - N can be 1,000 or 1M; tunable
- **Co-location**
  - Random assignment spreads 3 viewers of video 1 over 3 servers, which all subscribe
  - Ideal: all viewers of a video on one server
  - Mega videos (160M viewers): spread over ~160 servers, not 500,000
  - Easy with the dispatcher: route the new viewer to where the video already is
  - With pub/sub: an L7 LB at the gateway reads videoId from the header, asks a ZooKeeper-like service, routes
    - At that point, "why not just use the dispatcher?"; both work
  - Write-up: L7 LB with consistent hashing on liveVideoId (NGINX, Envoy) (write-up)
- **Redis vs Kafka** for pub/sub (staff signal)
  - Kafka: high overhead to subscribe/unsubscribe
  - Users scroll the feed, joining and leaving streams rapidly
  - Redis pub/sub is in memory; handles this better
  - Write-up: Redis is fire-and-forget; fine since comments are persisted (write-up)

## 12. Deep dive: the database

- Writes: 1M videos × ~100 comments each (probably high; most get none)
- Daily estimate on the board: 1M × 100 × 48
  - Evan's on-the-spot math: first 480M, then "off by an order of magnitude," ~4–5B a day
- High write throughput needed
  - Sharded, well-scaled Postgres would work
  - Few relations; simple query on a videoId index sorted by createdAt
- Pick: **Cassandra**
  - Shard (partition key) by videoId; sort key createdAt
  - Great at high write throughput
  - Eventual consistency: a read replica may lack the newest comment; acceptable per NFR
  - The real-time push path makes up for it
- Write-up uses DynamoDB instead (write-up)

## 13. Write-up-only deep dives

### 13.1 Mega-streams (write-up)

- World Cup final: hundreds of millions of viewers, thousands of comments/s (write-up)
- 5,000 comments/s × 4 words ≈ War and Peace in under 30 s (write-up)
  - Last 20 on screen: each visible ~4 ms; nobody can read it
- Users feel the "vibe," not individual comments (write-up)
- Good: show a representative subset (write-up)
  - Sampling rate adapts: ~50% at 100/s, 1–2% at 5,000/s
  - Prioritize followed users, comments with reactions, verified accounts
  - Still millions of SSE connections; costly
- Great: CDN delivery with periodic snapshots (write-up)
  - Ring buffer of the last 100–200 comments per mega-stream
  - Every second, snapshot to Redis or the CDN origin; CDN caches at the edge
  - Clients poll the CDN each second; animate new comments over the interval
  - Flip from SSE above a threshold (e.g., 100K viewers or 500 comments/s)
  - Costs: 1–2 s latency (fine here); show your own comment locally at once
  - Hysteresis on the threshold to avoid flapping
- Sampling shows strong understanding; CDN shows staff thinking: requirements change at extreme scale (write-up)

### 13.2 Disconnections (write-up)

- Bad: ignore; reconnecting users miss reactions to the big play (write-up)
- Great: **Last-Event-ID** (write-up)
  - Each SSE event carries an ID (the comment ID)
  - Browser reconnects with the last ID; server replays what was missed
  - Or the client stores its last ID and calls `GET …?since={id}&limit=100`
  - UX: replay at 2–3× speed, or "You missed 47 comments"
  - Mobile: disconnect when backgrounded, catch up when foregrounded
  - Bound replay (~5 minutes); degrade for longer gaps
  - A different server after reconnect needs history: shared Redis cache
  - Dedupe by comment ID when SSE and HTTP catch-up overlap

## 14. Wrap-up and level expectations

- Key takeaways
  - WebSocket vs SSE: WebSocket is heavier and needed for ~1:1 two-way traffic; SSE is lighter, server-to-client only
  - Scale with pub/sub or a central dispatcher to find which realtime server holds the connection
  - Same pattern as a real-time messaging app
  - Database scaling; the in-memory connection map
- Levels (from section 10 plus write-up)
  - Mid-level: realize polling's limits, move to push; reach pub/sub with minor hints (write-up)
  - Senior: speed through HLD; reach pub/sub with minimal hints; lead the scaling talk (write-up)
  - Staff: find pub/sub and call out its reliability/scaling limits with fixes; know exact technologies (write-up)
- Write-up's pick: pub/sub with co-location is easier with fewer corner cases (write-up)

## 15. Board as text (assembled from the talk)

```
Client --POST/GET--> API Gateway --> Comment Service (cache) --> Comments DB
   ^                                     |                     (Cassandra,
   |                                     v                      shard videoId,
   +---SSE--- Realtime Comment Svc <-- pub/sub                  SK createdAt)
              (~1,000; map videoId    hash(videoId) % N
               -> [conn...])
   Alt: Comment Service -> ZooKeeper (server/video registry) -> Realtime Svc
```

- Post path: POST, comment service writes DB, publishes to the video's channel
- Push path: subscribed realtime servers check their map, push over SSE
- History: GET with cursor and direction=before
- Board notes: WebSocket (bidirectional, own protocol, all infra must support upgrade) vs SSE (unidirectional, over HTTP, browser reconnection, chunked)
- ZooKeeper state example: servers with host, status, video connection counts; video to servers map
